rationale: The BOOK ENTRY makes a lexical claim, not a doctrinal one: that English 'hell' is a translation umbrella with no single scriptural referent, and that meaning must be recovered from the underlying word (Sheol, Hades, Gehenna, tartaroo). The printed proof texts carry exactly this claim. Psalm 16:10 puts the Messiah's own soul in 'hell' (Sheol), and Acts 2:27 quotes the same verse with Greek Hades — simultaneously proving that 'hell' translates Sheol, that Hades is the Greek equivalent of Sheol, and that this 'hell' cannot be the place of final punishment of the damned (the Holy One was there and was brought out). Matthew 10:28 uses Gehenna, a distinct word with a known geographic referent (the Valley of Hinnom, Jer 7:31-32). 2 Peter 2:4 uses the hapax tartaroo for angels held for future judgment — a third distinct referent, since angels reserved 'unto judgment' are by definition not yet in final punishment, and Jude 6 corroborates with 'chains of darkness.' No single referent can be true of all four printed texts without contradiction, which is precisely the entry's core claim. The strongest counter — that 'hell' properly denotes one thing, the final state of eternal conscious punishment — cannot explain Christ's presence in 'hell' in Ps 16:10/Acts 2:27 or the pre-judgment custody of 2 Pet 2:4 without either contradiction or conceding the entry's point that these are different underlying words. Notably, the common-interpretation surveys themselves (Responses A and C) concede the lexical distinction as a 'common' reading that is 'standard in academic biblical studies and modern translations.' Every material assertion actually printed in the entry is supported; the chapter's further doctrinal arguments (annihilationism, fire-as-God, Platonic genealogy) are chapter-only and out of scope.
book_core_identification: 'Hell' is an ambiguous English translation label with no single scriptural referent; its meaning in any passage must be taken from the underlying Hebrew or Greek word it translates (Sheol, Hades, Gehenna, or tartaroo).
book_secondary_elaborations: Alias mapping: 'hell' translating Sheol refers to Sheol (the grave/realm of the dead).
Alias mapping: 'hell' translating Hades also refers to Sheol, i.e., Hades is treated as the Greek equivalent of Hebrew Sheol.
Alias mapping: 'hell' translating Gehenna refers to Gehenna, the Valley of Hinnom.
Alias mapping: 'hell' translating tartaroo (2 Pet 2:4) refers to Tartarus.
chapter_only_objections: The chapter's annihilationist/conditionalist doctrine (second death as final uncreation, 'as though they had not been') is a doctrinal claim beyond the entry's lexical scope and is contested by traditionalist readings of Rev 14:10-11 and 20:10.
The claim that hell-fire is not a place at all but the unshielded presence of God ('our God is a consuming fire') is a theological construction not asserted in the entry.
The historical genealogy tracing endless-torment doctrine to Plato via Philo, Tertullian, and Augustine is a historiographical argument outside the entry.
The etymological argument that kolasis (Matt 25:46) means gardener's pruning and hence terminal destruction is disputed lexically and appears only in the chapter.
The reading of Luke 16 (rich man and Lazarus) as a parable whose imagery cannot inform afterlife doctrine is a chapter-level hermeneutical claim.
The appeal to the Cochin Hebrew Revelation manuscripts ('acher maveth') and Aramaic Targum parallels is text-critically idiosyncratic and appears only in the chapter.
The argument from Deuteronomy 28's silence and the law's punishment caps (Deut 25:3) to the impossibility of endless torment is a chapter-level inference.
The soul-mortality argument (Gen 2:7; Ezek 18:4; 1 Tim 6:16) is chapter doctrine, not printed in the entry.
strongest_counter_interpretation: The traditionalist reading (Responses B and D): 'Hell' denotes a single coherent referent — the final place/state of eternal conscious punishment and separation from God for the unrighteous and fallen angels — with the various biblical terms (Hades, Gehenna, Tartarus, lake of fire) functioning as aspects or stages of one unified doctrine of hell, so that the English word legitimately names one theological reality rather than being an ambiguous umbrella requiring word-by-word disambiguation.
counter_core_identification: 'Hell' has a single scriptural referent: the final state of eternal conscious punishment and separation from God, of which the different underlying terms are facets or phases.
material_core_denial: The counter denies the entry's core by asserting that English 'hell' does have a single scriptural referent (final eternal punishment), so that its meaning need not — and should not — be dissolved into distinct underlying words.
counter_case: Jesus' Gehenna warnings (Mark 9:43-48; Matt 5:22) and the lake of fire (Rev 20:10-15) plausibly describe one final destiny, so unifying them under 'hell' is theologically coherent.
Luke 16:23 depicts conscious torment in Hades, arguably blurring the Hades/Gehenna boundary the entry insists on.
2 Pet 2:4 and Jude 6 concern judgment on angels, which Matt 25:41 ('eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels') links to the same final fire, suggesting continuity among the terms.
Centuries of Catholic, Orthodox, and Protestant usage treat 'hell' as a unified doctrinal term, and the KJV translators deliberately rendered all these words 'hell.'
book_explanatory_advantages: Ps 16:10/Acts 2:27 place the Messiah's soul in 'hell' and promise his release — inexplicable if 'hell' means final eternal punishment, but exactly expected if this 'hell' is Sheol/Hades, the grave, from which resurrection retrieves him (Peter's own Pentecost argument).
The Ps 16:10 → Acts 2:27 quotation chain directly demonstrates the entry's Hades→Sheol equivalence: the same verse uses Sheol in Hebrew and Hades in Greek.

2 Pet 2:4 uses a unique verb (tartaroo) and describes custody 'reserved unto judgment' — a holding state prior to judgment, not final punishment — which the single-referent view cannot accommodate without equivocation; Jude 6 confirms the pre-judgment custody reading.

Matt 10:28 speaks of destroying soul and body in Gehenna — a named, geographically grounded term (Valley of Hinnom, Jer 7:31-32) distinct from the Hades that 'delivered up the dead' before itself being destroyed (Rev 20:13-14), a verse that is incoherent if Hades and the lake of fire are the same 'hell.'

The KJV's own split rendering of Sheol (31x 'grave,' 31x 'hell') and Rev 20:13-14's casting of Hades into the lake of fire independently corroborate that the English label conflates distinct referents.

The entry's position matches what even the common-interpretation surveys (Responses A and C) classify as a 'common' reading, standard in academic biblical studies and reflected in modern translations that transliterate rather than render 'hell.'
counter_explanatory_advantages: The counter preserves continuity with the dominant historical doctrine and reads Luke 16:23's torment-in-Hades imagery at face value.
It offers a simpler pastoral vocabulary: one word, one destiny, without lexical disambiguation.
decisive_sources: Psalm 16:10 with Acts 2:27 — the same verse rendering Sheol as Hades, and 'hell' as the place the Holy One entered and left, which cannot be final punishment
Revelation 20:13-14 (cited via the chapter and Response A/C) — Hades delivered up its dead and was itself cast into the lake of fire, formally distinguishing two things the English word conflates
2 Peter 2:4 with Jude 6 — tartaroo as pre-judgment custody of angels, a third distinct referent
Matthew 10:28 — Gehenna as the locus of destruction of soul and body, distinct from the grave-Hades of Acts 2:27
Jeremiah 7:31-32 background for Gehenna as the Valley of Hinnom (acknowledged in Responses A and C as standard scholarship)
unresolved_objections: Luke 16:23's depiction of conscious torment in Hades sits awkwardly with the chapter's silent-sleep characterization of Sheol/Hades, though the entry itself makes no claim about the interior condition of Sheol, so this objection weighs on the chapter, not the printed entry.
Whether Gehenna and the lake of fire are ultimately the same final judgment is left open by the entry, which only maps the words; this underdetermination does not defeat the lexical claim.
